title: Grade 4 ENGLISH LANGUAGE — 2.2.1 Reading: Intensive Reading

pages.lesson:
PAGE 1: Overview

OVERVIEW
========

Intensive reading means reading a poem or story carefully so that you understand it. In this sub-strand you will use the title and pictures, follow events in order, notice similes and sayings, and answer questions whose answers are written in the text and questions that need you to think.

## Strand 2.0: Family Celebrations
Sub-strand 2.2.1: Reading: Intensive Reading
Suggested lessons: 3

## Learning outcomes
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) read poems or stories related to the theme for comprehension
b) apply appropriate reading techniques to answer direct and indirect questions based on a poem or story for self- expression
c) realise the importance of reading comprehension for lifelong learning

## What this sub-strand covers
• Poems
• Stories
• Similes and sayings
• Reading techniques

## Key inquiry questions
1. Why should we read the title and pictures in a story?
2. What is your favourite poem or story?

## Core competencies
• Self-efficacy: This is developed as the learner is able to identify and talk about events in a story logically and fluently.
• Learning to learn: It is enhanced as the learner uses appropriate reading techniques to answer questions appropriately.

## Values
• Social justice: This is promoted as the learner fosters fairness by allowing equal opportunities to peers when participating in a readers' theatre.
• Responsibility: This is enhanced as the learner engages in assigned roles and duties diligently.

## Pertinent and contemporary issues
• Self-esteem: It is developed as the learner gains confidence as they recite poems or stories with peers.

## Links to other learning areas
• The learner is able to link the concept of reading poems and songs to their learning in Creative Arts.

## Source
• KICD Grade 4 English Language Curriculum Design (Revised 2024) — Theme 2.0 Family Celebrations, Sub-strand 2.2.1 Intensive Reading

PAGE 2: Lesson 1: Reading a poem: similes and a saying

LESSON 1: READING A POEM: SIMILES AND A SAYING
==============================================

## What you will learn
• Use the title and a picture to predict what a poem is about.
• Read a poem about a birthday and find its similes and saying.
• Answer a direct question and an indirect question about the poem.

Curriculum outcomes: a) read poems or stories related to the theme for comprehension; b) apply appropriate reading techniques to answer direct and indirect questions based on a poem or story for self- expression

## Introduction
Before you read a single line, the title already gives you a clue. The Birthday Morning tells you the time and the event. A picture of balloons and a cake would tell you even more. Good readers look before they start.

## Notes
### Look first
Intensive reading begins before the first sentence. Read the title. Look at any picture or diagram. Ask: Who might be in this text? Where is it happening? What might go wrong or go well?

The poem below is called The Birthday Morning. Picture a kitchen table, a cake, balloons on the wall, and a family clearing plates together. That picture prepares you for the words.

### Two tools inside the poem
A simile compares two things using like or as. It helps the reader see or hear the scene.

- as busy as a beehive
- as sweet as a ripe mango
- like bright fruit

A saying is a short familiar sentence that carries advice or a truth. In this poem Grandfather says, "Many hands make light work." It means a job is easier when many people share it.

### The poem
The Birthday Morning

The kitchen was as busy as a beehive.
The cake was as sweet as a ripe mango.
Balloons hung like bright fruit on the walls.
Ribbons shone as red as the evening sun.

We sang a song as loud as the rain,
Then laughed like chicks set free in the yard.
Grandfather's smile was as warm as tea.
He said, "Many hands make light work,"
And every child helped to clear the plates.

A gift can be as small as a card,
But being together was the best present of all.

### Direct and indirect questions
A direct question is answered by words that are written in the text. What did Grandfather say? He said, "Many hands make light work." You can point to the line.

An indirect question makes you think. Why was being together the best present? The poem does not say "because" in one neat sentence. You use clues: the family sang, laughed, helped and stayed together. The best present was the people, not only the card.

### How to recite
Stand tall, hold the page below your face, and speak so the back of the room can hear. Pause at the end of a line when the sense pauses. Stress the comparing words like and as so the similes stand out. Then ask a partner one oral question.

## Key words
• simile — a comparison that uses like or as
• saying — a short familiar sentence that gives advice or a truth
• direct question — a question whose answer is written in the text
• indirect question — a question you answer by thinking about clues in the text

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Find two similes in the first four lines of The Birthday Morning.

Working:
1. Look for like or as.
2. "As busy as a beehive" compares the kitchen to a beehive.
3. "As sweet as a ripe mango" compares the cake to a mango.

Answer: as busy as a beehive; as sweet as a ripe mango

### Example 2
Is "What saying did Grandfather use?" a direct or an indirect question?

Working:
1. The poem writes the exact words he said.
2. You can point to the line.

Answer: Direct. He said, "Many hands make light work."

## Activity: Title, picture, poem
You will need: The poem The Birthday Morning, The diagram of the birthday table, Exercise books
1. Before reading, talk about the title and the picture. Say what you expect to find in the poem.
2. Read the poem silently, then aloud with your group.
3. Underline every simile and the saying. Compare your list with a partner.
4. Recite two lines each. Then answer one direct question and one indirect question orally.

## Practice
1. What is the poem's title, and what does it tell you before you read?
2. Quote the saying in the poem.
3. Why do the children clear the plates?
4. What does the simile "Grandfather's smile was as warm as tea" help you understand?

## Summary
• Read the title and look at the picture before you read the words.
• A simile uses like or as. A saying gives a short truth.
• Direct answers are written in the text. Indirect answers use clues.

### Answers to practice
1. The Birthday Morning. It tells you the poem is about a birthday and that it happens in the morning.
2. Many hands make light work.
3. Grandfather says many hands make light work, and every child helps. Sharing the job makes it easier.
4. His smile made people feel warm and welcome, the way a cup of tea does.

PAGE 3: Lesson 2: Reading a story and keeping the events in order

LESSON 2: READING A STORY AND KEEPING THE EVENTS IN ORDER
=========================================================

## What you will learn
• Read a short story about a family wedding.
• List the events in the order they happen.
• Answer direct and indirect questions about the story.

Curriculum outcomes: a) read poems or stories related to the theme for comprehension; b) apply appropriate reading techniques to answer direct and indirect questions based on a poem or story for self- expression

## Introduction
Stories make sense when events stay in order. If you say the guests arrived before you say who was getting married, the listener is lost. Careful reading follows the path the writer made.

## Notes
### The story
A Card for Aunt Achieng

Aunt Achieng was getting married on Saturday. On Friday evening the children sat under a tree and planned their part. Musa said he would carry the flowers. Amina said she would help with the cake. Their cousin Joy held up a small card. "It says, We wish you joy," she told them.

On Saturday the compound was as colourful as a market of flowers. Guests came with gifts and songs. The children stood in a line and sang. Aunt Achieng's dress was as white as clouds, and her smile was as bright as a lamp.

After the ceremony, Grandmother called the children close. "A family that celebrates together grows closer," she said. Musa gave Aunt Achieng the card. She read it and hugged the three children. "This card is as precious as any gift," she said.

That night the children were tired but full of joy. They had learnt that a celebration is not only cake and balloons. It is the people who come, the songs they sing, and the kind words they share.

### Events in order
Write the events as a chain, not as a pile.

1. On Friday the children plan: flowers, cake and a card.
2. On Saturday the guests arrive and the children sing.
3. After the ceremony Grandmother speaks and the card is given.
4. At night the children think about what a celebration really is.

If you swap 1 and 3, the card appears before it has been made. Order keeps the story fluent.

### Similes and a saying in the story
Similes: as colourful as a market of flowers; as white as clouds; as bright as a lamp; as precious as any gift.

Saying: "A family that celebrates together grows closer." Grandmother uses it to teach the children. You can agree with a saying and still explain it in your own words.

### Questions
Direct: What did Joy's card say? It said, "We wish you joy."

Direct: When was the wedding? On Saturday.

Indirect: Why did Aunt Achieng call the card precious? The story shows that she hugged the children after reading their kind words. The card mattered because of the love behind it, not because it cost money. The text gives the clues. You put them together.

### Readers' theatre
In a readers' theatre you read the story aloud in parts. You do not need costumes. You need a clear voice and a fair turn. Narrator, Musa, Amina, Joy, Grandmother and Aunt Achieng can each take a share. Everyone should have a chance to read.

## Key words
• event — something that happens in a story
• order — the sequence from first to last
• readers' theatre — reading a story aloud in parts, with each person taking a role

## Worked examples

### Example 1
What did the children decide on Friday evening?

Working:
1. Look at the first paragraph.
2. Musa, Amina and Joy each name a job.

Answer: Musa would carry flowers, Amina would help with the cake, and Joy had made a card.

### Example 2
Why is "What did the children learn about celebrations?" an indirect question?

Working:
1. The last paragraph does not use the word learn in a single quoted fact only.
2. The reader must join the last sentences: a celebration is people, songs and kind words, not only cake and balloons.

Answer: The answer is not one copied label. You explain the idea the ending gives.

## Activity: Readers' theatre
You will need: Copies of A Card for Aunt Achieng, A pencil to mark parts
1. Read the story silently and number the four main events.
2. With your group, mark parts: narrator, Musa, Amina, Joy, Grandmother and Aunt Achieng.
3. Give every learner a turn. Read the story aloud in those parts.
4. Answer two oral questions, one direct and one indirect, and point to the paragraph that helped you.

## Practice
1. When did the children sit under the tree to plan?
2. What saying did Grandmother use?
3. Put these events in order: the children sing; Joy shows the card; Aunt Achieng hugs the children.
4. Why did Aunt Achieng value the card?

## Summary
• Follow events from the first plan to the last lesson of the story.
• Similes and sayings add pictures and advice.
• In readers' theatre, every reader needs a fair turn.

### Answers to practice
1. On Friday evening.
2. A family that celebrates together grows closer.
3. Joy shows the card; the children sing; Aunt Achieng hugs the children.
4. It carried the children's kind wishes. She said it was as precious as any gift, and she hugged them.

PAGE 4: Lesson 3: Reading techniques that last

LESSON 3: READING TECHNIQUES THAT LAST
======================================

## What you will learn
• Use a simple set of reading techniques on a poem or story.
• Role-play one event from a text about a celebration.
• Explain why reading for understanding helps you outside school.

Curriculum outcomes: b) apply appropriate reading techniques to answer direct and indirect questions based on a poem or story for self- expression; c) realise the importance of reading comprehension for lifelong learning

## Introduction
A reader who only slides their eyes over words can finish a page and still not know what happened. A reader who uses a few steady techniques can retell the piece, answer questions, and use the idea again later.

## Notes
### A technique is a habit
These steps work for poems, stories and most school texts.

1. Preview. Read the title and look at pictures. Guess the topic.
2. Read once for the story. Do not stop for every new word.
3. Track the events in order. A quick numbered list is enough.
4. Collect new words, similes and sayings. Ask what each one adds.
5. Answer direct questions by pointing to the line.
6. Answer indirect questions by joining clues. Start your answer with "I think" only if you then give the clue.
7. Retell the text in a few sentences of your own.

### Try the steps on one line
From the poem: "Balloons hung like bright fruit on the walls."

- Direct: Where were the balloons? On the walls.
- The simile compares balloons to bright fruit, so the room looked colourful.
- You do not need a dictionary for like in this line. The comparison itself tells you the picture.

From the story: "This card is as precious as any gift."

- Precious means of great value.
- The simile tells you the handmade card mattered as much as the other presents.

### Role-play to test understanding
Choose one event, such as the moment Musa gives the card. Act it in two minutes. If you can show what happened and how people felt, you have understood that part. If the scene is confused, read the paragraph again before you act.

### Why this skill stays with you
You will meet invitations, stories, songs and news for the rest of your life. Understanding them keeps you from missing a time, a place or a feeling. Reading for meaning also grows your words, so the next text is easier than the last. That is lifelong learning: each careful reading teaches you how to read the one after it.

Share the reading. When a group watches a short video of a family celebration, listen for one fact and one feeling. The same techniques work on a screen as on a page: title or opening picture first, then events, then what they mean.

## Key words
• preview — to look at the title and pictures before reading the whole text
• retell — to say a text again in your own words
• lifelong learning — keeping on learning after the lesson and after school

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A learner answers "Where did the balloons hang?" with "I think in a shop." What should the learner do instead?

Working:
1. This is a direct question.
2. The poem says the balloons hung on the walls.
3. Point to the line instead of guessing a new place.

Answer: Answer from the text: on the walls.

### Example 2
Give one reason reading for understanding will help you after you leave this class.

Working:
1. Think of real texts: invitations, stories, instructions.
2. Missing the meaning can mean missing the event or the message.

Answer: You can understand invitations, stories and other texts you meet later, and each text makes the next one easier.

## Activity: Act one event, then retell
You will need: The poem and the story from this sub-strand, Space to role-play, A video of a celebration only if the teacher provides one
1. Choose either the poem or the story. Preview the title again and list the events in order.
2. Discuss one event and role-play it. Give each person a part.
3. Answer one direct question by pointing to the sentence, and one indirect question by naming your clue.
4. If a video is available, watch it for one fact about a celebration and tell the class that fact in your own words.

## Practice
1. List the first three reading techniques from this lesson, in order.
2. Is "Where were the balloons?" direct or indirect? Give the answer.
3. What does "as precious as any gift" tell you about the card?
4. Why is reading for understanding useful beyond one English lesson?

## Summary
• Preview, read, order the events, collect similes and sayings, then answer both kinds of questions.
• Role-play is a test of whether you understood an event.
• Careful reading is a skill you keep using all your life.

### Answers to practice
1. Preview the title and pictures; read once for the story; track the events in order.
2. Direct. They hung on the walls.
3. The card was as valuable as the other presents.
4. It helps you understand texts you meet in life, and each careful reading makes the next one easier.
pages.quiz:
REVISION QUIZ — 2.2.1 READING: INTENSIVE READING
========================================

Answer all the questions, then mark yourself on the Answers tab.

1. What should you look at before you read a story?
   A. Only the last line
   B. The title and the pictures
   C. The page number alone
   D. Someone else's answers

2. Which phrase is a simile?
   A. Many hands make light work
   B. as sweet as a ripe mango
   C. The children sang
   D. on Saturday morning

3. What saying does Grandfather use in the poem?
   A. Better late than never
   B. Many hands make light work
   C. A stitch in time
   D. Look before you leap

4. What did Joy's card say?

5. Which event happened first?
   A. Aunt Achieng hugged the children
   B. The children sang at the wedding
   C. The children planned under the tree on Friday
   D. Grandmother spoke after the ceremony

6. Why is "Why did Aunt Achieng value the card?" an indirect question?

7. What does "as white as clouds" describe?
   A. The cake
   B. The card
   C. Aunt Achieng's dress
   D. The flowers Musa carried

8. In readers' theatre, what should the group make sure of?
   A. Only the fastest reader speaks
   B. Each person gets a fair turn
   C. Nobody looks at the text
   D. The ending is read first

9. Where did the balloons hang in the poem?
   A. In the shop
   B. On the walls
   C. Under the tree
   D. On the cake

10. Why is reading for understanding a lifelong skill?
pages.answers:
ANSWERS — 2.2.1 READING: INTENSIVE READING
========================================

1. B. The title and the pictures
   The title and pictures help you predict the topic.

2. B. as sweet as a ripe mango
   A simile compares using like or as. This one uses as.

3. B. Many hands make light work
   He says it just before the children clear the plates.

4. We wish you joy.
   The story states the words on the card. This is a direct answer.

5. C. The children planned under the tree on Friday
   The planning on Friday evening comes before Saturday's wedding.

6. The story does not give a single labelled reason. You join clues: the kind words, the hug, and her saying the card was as precious as any gift.
   Indirect questions need thinking, not only copying one line.

7. C. Aunt Achieng's dress
   The story says her dress was as white as clouds.

8. B. Each person gets a fair turn
   Fair turns let every learner read.

9. B. On the walls
   The line says balloons hung like bright fruit on the walls.

10. You keep meeting texts such as stories and invitations, and each careful reading makes the next one easier.
   Comprehension is useful beyond a single lesson.

LESSON 2: READING A STORY AND KEEPING THE EVENTS IN ORDER
=========================================================

## What you will learn
• Read a short story about a family wedding.
• List the events in the order they happen.
• Answer direct and indirect questions about the story.

Curriculum outcomes: a) read poems or stories related to the theme for comprehension; b) apply appropriate reading techniques to answer direct and indirect questions based on a poem or story for self- expression

## Introduction
Stories make sense when events stay in order. If you say the guests arrived before you say who was getting married, the listener is lost. Careful reading follows the path the writer made.

## Notes
### The story
A Card for Aunt Achieng

Aunt Achieng was getting married on Saturday. On Friday evening the children sat under a tree and planned their part. Musa said he would carry the flowers. Amina said she would help with the cake. Their cousin Joy held up a small card. "It says, We wish you joy," she told them.

### Events in order
Write the events as a chain, not as a pile.

1. On Friday the children plan: flowers, cake and a card.
2. On Saturday the guests arrive and the children sing.
3. After the ceremony Grandmother speaks and the card is given.
4. At night the children think about what a celebration really is.

If you swap 1 and 3, the card appears before it has been made. Order keeps the story fluent.

### Similes and a saying in the story
Similes: as colourful as a market of flowers; as white as clouds; as bright as a lamp; as precious as any gift.

Saying: "A family that celebrates together grows closer." Grandmother uses it to teach the children. You can agree with a saying and still explain it in your own words.

### Questions
Direct: What did Joy's card say? It said, "We wish you joy."

Direct: When was the wedding? On Saturday.

Indirect: Why did Aunt Achieng call the card precious? The story shows that she hugged the children after reading their kind words. The card mattered because of the love behind it, not because it cost money. The text gives the clues. You put them together.

### Readers' theatre
In a readers' theatre you read the story aloud in parts. You do not need costumes. You need a clear voice and a fair turn. Narrator, Musa, Amina, Joy, Grandmother and Aunt Achieng can each take a share. Everyone should have a chance to read.

## Key words
• event — something that happens in a story
• order — the sequence from first to last
• readers' theatre — reading a story aloud in parts, with each person taking a role

## Worked examples

### Example 1
What did the children decide on Friday evening?

Working:
1. Look at the first paragraph.
2. Musa, Amina and Joy each name a job.

Answer: Musa would carry flowers, Amina would help with the cake, and Joy had made a card.

### Example 2
Why is "What did the children learn about celebrations?" an indirect question?

Working:
1. The last paragraph does not use the word learn in a single quoted fact only.
2. The reader must join the last sentences: a celebration is people, songs and kind words, not only cake and balloons.

Answer: The answer is not one copied label. You explain the idea the ending gives.

## Activity: Readers' theatre
You will need: Copies of A Card for Aunt Achieng, A pencil to mark parts
1. Read the story silently and number the four main events.
2. With your group, mark parts: narrator, Musa, Amina, Joy, Grandmother and Aunt Achieng.
3. Give every learner a turn. Read the story aloud in those parts.
4. Answer two oral questions, one direct and one indirect, and point to the paragraph that helped you.

## Practice
1. When did the children sit under the tree to plan?
2. What saying did Grandmother use?
3. Put these events in order: the children sing; Joy shows the card; Aunt Achieng hugs the children.
4. Why did Aunt Achieng value the card?

## Summary
• Follow events from the first plan to the last lesson of the story.
• Similes and sayings add pictures and advice.
• In readers' theatre, every reader needs a fair turn.

### Answers to practice
1. On Friday evening.
2. A family that celebrates together grows closer.
3. Joy shows the card; the children sing; Aunt Achieng hugs the children.
4. It carried the children's kind wishes. She said it was as precious as any gift, and she hugged them.

studyPages.title: Lesson 3: Reading techniques that last
studyPages.body:
LESSON 3: READING TECHNIQUES THAT LAST
======================================

## What you will learn
• Use a simple set of reading techniques on a poem or story.
• Role-play one event from a text about a celebration.
• Explain why reading for understanding helps you outside school.

Curriculum outcomes: b) apply appropriate reading techniques to answer direct and indirect questions based on a poem or story for self- expression; c) realise the importance of reading comprehension for lifelong learning

## Introduction
A reader who only slides their eyes over words can finish a page and still not know what happened. A reader who uses a few steady techniques can retell the piece, answer questions, and use the idea again later.

## Notes
### A technique is a habit
These steps work for poems, stories and most school texts.

1. Preview. Read the title and look at pictures. Guess the topic.
2. Read once for the story. Do not stop for every new word.
3. Track the events in order. A quick numbered list is enough.
4. Collect new words, similes and sayings. Ask what each one adds.
5. Answer direct questions by pointing to the line.
6. Answer indirect questions by joining clues. Start your answer with "I think" only if you then give the clue.
7. Retell the text in a few sentences of your own.

### Try the steps on one line
From the poem: "Balloons hung like bright fruit on the walls."

- Direct: Where were the balloons? On the walls.
- The simile compares balloons to bright fruit, so the room looked colourful.
- You do not need a dictionary for like in this line. The comparison itself tells you the picture.

From the story: "This card is as precious as any gift."

- Precious means of great value.
- The simile tells you the handmade card mattered as much as the other presents.

### Role-play to test understanding
Choose one event, such as the moment Musa gives the card. Act it in two minutes. If you can show what happened and how people felt, you have understood that part. If the scene is confused, read the paragraph again before you act.

### Why this skill stays with you
You will meet invitations, stories, songs and news for the rest of your life. Understanding them keeps you from missing a time, a place or a feeling. Reading for meaning also grows your words, so the next text is easier than the last. That is lifelong learning: each careful reading teaches you how to read the one after it.

Share the reading. When a group watches a short video of a family celebration, listen for one fact and one feeling. The same techniques work on a screen as on a page: title or opening picture first, then events, then what they mean.

## Key words
• preview — to look at the title and pictures before reading the whole text
• retell — to say a text again in your own words
• lifelong learning — keeping on learning after the lesson and after school

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A learner answers "Where did the balloons hang?" with "I think in a shop." What should the learner do instead?

Working:
1. This is a direct question.
2. The poem says the balloons hung on the walls.
3. Point to the line instead of guessing a new place.

Answer: Answer from the text: on the walls.

### Example 2
Give one reason reading for understanding will help you after you leave this class.

Working:
1. Think of real texts: invitations, stories, instructions.
2. Missing the meaning can mean missing the event or the message.

Answer: You can understand invitations, stories and other texts you meet later, and each text makes the next one easier.

## Activity: Act one event, then retell
You will need: The poem and the story from this sub-strand, Space to role-play, A video of a celebration only if the teacher provides one
1. Choose either the poem or the story. Preview the title again and list the events in order.
2. Discuss one event and role-play it. Give each person a part.
3. Answer one direct question by pointing to the sentence, and one indirect question by naming your clue.
4. If a video is available, watch it for one fact about a celebration and tell the class that fact in your own words.

## Practice
1. List the first three reading techniques from this lesson, in order.
2. Is "Where were the balloons?" direct or indirect? Give the answer.
3. What does "as precious as any gift" tell you about the card?
4. Why is reading for understanding useful beyond one English lesson?

## Summary
• Preview, read, order the events, collect similes and sayings, then answer both kinds of questions.
• Role-play is a test of whether you understood an event.
• Careful reading is a skill you keep using all your life.

### Answers to practice
1. Preview the title and pictures; read once for the story; track the events in order.
2. Direct. They hung on the walls.
3. The card was as valuable as the other presents.
4. It helps you understand texts you meet in life, and each careful reading makes the next one easier.

questions.question: What should you look at before you read a story?
questions.explanation: The title and pictures help you predict the topic.

questions.question: Which phrase is a simile?
options: as sweet as a ripe mango
questions.explanation: A simile compares using like or as. This one uses as.

questions.question: What saying does Grandfather use in the poem?
questions.explanation: He says it just before the children clear the plates.

questions.question: What did Joy's card say?
questions.explanation: The story states the words on the card. This is a direct answer.

questions.question: Which event happened first?
options: The children sang at the wedding
The children planned under the tree on Friday
questions.explanation: The planning on Friday evening comes before Saturday's wedding.

questions.question: Why is "Why did Aunt Achieng value the card?" an indirect question?
questions.answer: The story does not give a single labelled reason. You join clues: the kind words, the hug, and her saying the card was as precious as any gift.
questions.explanation: Indirect questions need thinking, not only copying one line.

questions.question: What does "as white as clouds" describe?
questions.explanation: The story says her dress was as white as clouds.

questions.question: In readers' theatre, what should the group make sure of?
options: Each person gets a fair turn
questions.explanation: Fair turns let every learner read.

questions.question: Where did the balloons hang in the poem?
questions.explanation: The line says balloons hung like bright fruit on the walls.

questions.question: Why is reading for understanding a lifelong skill?
questions.answer: You keep meeting texts such as stories and invitations, and each careful reading makes the next one easier.
questions.explanation: Comprehension is useful beyond a single lesson.
